overview: The Iceland label begins in 1900, while the island was under the Danish crown. Home rule expanded in 1904, Iceland became a sovereign kingdom sharing Denmark’s monarch in 1918, and the republic was founded in 1944. Modern Iceland’s history combines fishing, public institutions and inventive uses of geothermal heat.

periods.title: Toward home rule and sovereignty
periods.summary: Home-rule changes took effect in 1904 while Iceland remained connected to Denmark.

periods.title: The sovereign kingdom
periods.summary: The Union Act recognized Iceland as a sovereign state in a personal union with Denmark.

periods.title: The republic
periods.summary: The republic was established at Þingvellir on 17 June 1944.

sections.title: Learning, work and shared public life

items.text: The University of Iceland opened in 1911 by bringing together schools of theology, medicine and law, with an additional philosophy faculty. Its first academic year enrolled forty-five students, including one woman. An institution that would later grow much larger began with a very small student body.

For its first twenty-nine years, the university occupied space in Parliament House. It moved into its own main building in 1940. Early students and professors therefore learned and taught in a building whose other job was running the country’s parliamentary business.

At Siglufjörður, the Róaldsbrakki herring station dates from 1907. Its surviving rooms include accommodation for young women who came for seasonal processing work. The museum preserves the close relationship between earning a living, temporary housing and the summer fishing industry.

On 24 October 1975, many Icelandic women stopped both paid work and household work for a day. Meetings and singing accompanied the protest. The Women’s History Archives preserves the event as a demonstration of how much ordinary society depended on women’s labor.

Heated outdoor swimming pools are gathering places in Iceland, even in a cold climate. UNESCO’s account describes hot tubs as settings for informal debate and conversation. A discussion about the day’s news can happen while everyone is sitting comfortably in warm water.

Swimming skills and pool customs pass between generations through family visits, lessons and school activities. The 2025 UNESCO decision notes the requirement for swimming lessons for children aged six to sixteen. Learning to swim is part of growing up within this public culture.

sections.title: Heat beneath the ground, and people above it

items.text: Women in Reykjavík carried washing along the route called Laugavegur to the hot springs, using their natural heat for laundry. The work could involve a three-kilometer journey and heavy loads. Hot water was useful long before it arrived conveniently through a pipe at home.

In 1930, a pipeline supplied geothermal water to public buildings near Reykjavík’s laundry springs. Later household district heating reduced the need to tend coal fires. Historian Odinn Melsted also shows that access spread unevenly and that easier heating did not make all the other housework disappear.

When Eldfell erupted beside Heimaey’s town in January 1973, nearly all its residents were evacuated within six hours. A prepared civil-defense plan and the fishing fleet in port helped people reach the mainland. Boats normally used for earning a living became essential rescue transport.

Crews sprayed seawater on the advancing lava during the Heimaey eruption. Cooling helped slow or divert some flows and reduce damage. The US Geological Survey stresses the special circumstances: a slow-moving flow, nearby seawater and good access for pumps and equipment.

The 1944 republic ceremony at Þingvellir needed buses, repaired roads, tents and a stage for performances. Visitors endured wind and rain, and the proclamation was carried by radio. Creating a national celebration involved transport and shelter as well as speeches and flags.

Icelandic, article 1 of the 1944 constitution: “Ísland er lýðveldi með þingbundinni stjórn.” Translation: “Iceland is a republic with a parliamentary government.” This excerpt follows Alþingi’s official 2024 consolidated edition of the law that took effect on 17 June 1944.

ending.text: Iceland continues as a republic. The 1944 change ended the shared monarchy with Denmark; it followed sovereignty in 1918 and earlier home rule. The map’s 1900 starting point therefore precedes both the sovereign kingdom and the republic.
